digest.intro: AI solves a Millennium Problem, steals credit, and may kill us all.

items.title: AI Has Solved One of Math's $1 Million Millennium Prize Problems
items.blurb: 10,000 autonomous OpenAI agents running an unreleased model found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations — one of the six remaining Millennium Prize Problems — in 88 hours, then formally verified the proof in Lean. The fluid dynamics equations have been central to physics since the mid-19th century; whether their solutions always stay well-behaved has been an open question the whole time. This is the primary source; read it first.

items.title: What OpenAI's Latest Controversy Tells Us About the Future of Math
items.blurb: OpenAI's Sébastien Bubeck admitted in a press briefing that the team was 'inspired to pursue the problem after hearing a rumor' about NYU's Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic's Levent Alpöge already working on it — which is doing a lot of work in one sentence. The deeper structural question Tech Review raises: if frontier AI math now requires resources only two or three companies can afford, and those companies absorb human mathematicians' unpublished leads without credit, what's left for academic math? That's not a hypothetical; it's this week.

items.title: Anthropic Researcher Quits With a Warning: Self-Improving AI Could 'Kill Us All'
items.blurb: Jacob Coxon's resignation post would be easy to dismiss as routine doom-posting, except Anthropic's own Alignment Science lead Evan Hubinger publicly seconded it, putting his personal estimate of AI killing all humans within a decade at greater than 10%. The timing — same week an Anthropic employee is at the center of the Navier-Stokes credit scandal, same week OpenAI's agents clear a Millennium Problem — makes this feel less like a warning and more like a dispatch from inside the acceleration.

items.title: Six Chinese AI Firms Accused of Aggressively Copying US Frontier Models
items.blurb: The NSA, CISA, and FBI jointly named DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.AI as running industrial-scale distillation attacks on US frontier models since at least late 2024 — bulk-buying fake accounts and firing coordinated prompt swarms ranging from thousands to millions of queries. The alleged goal: compress years of frontier training into months, at a fraction of the cost. The US response reportedly includes pressuring AI firms to secretly downgrade capabilities served to Chinese users, which is its own kind of epistemically interesting problem.

items.title: WeWorm: First Zero-Click Worm Spreading Through WeChat Calls on iOS and Android
items.blurb: The victim doesn't need to answer the call, doesn't need to touch their phone — the exploit succeeds regardless, silently. Calif Research says their team found the bug and wrote the first RCE exploit in about two days with AI assistance; the worm took one more week. The editorial note in their release is the part that should stay with you: 'A worm at this scale used to be the kind of thing that took a larger team months. AI can already do most of the work here.'

items.title: Google's AI Genome System Evaluates Every Possible One-Base Change
items.blurb: AlphaGenome Atlas ran 9 billion base substitutions — every possible single-nucleotide variant against the 3-billion-base human reference genome — through Google's AlphaGenome model, producing a systematic functional annotation of essentially every SNV in the human genome. The target is the 97%+ of the genome that doesn't encode proteins but controls when and where genes turn on; predicting which of those variants matter has been the core bottleneck in interpreting genetic disease. This is infrastructure, not a cure — but it's the kind of map that changes what questions you can even ask.

items.title: The Medieval Curio Cabinet of Mental Health
items.blurb: Medieval physicians treating what we'd now call mental illness prescribed saffron, ostrich liver, carefully designed gardens, music, and structured animal contact — not only exorcism, which tends to dominate the popular imagination. The essay argues that medieval medicine, read without condescension, shows a surprisingly coherent environmental and sensory model of psychological treatment that holds up better under modern environmental psychology than its reputation suggests. A 29-minute rabbit hole that will make you reconsider what 'superstitious' actually means as a category.

facts.fact: Anthropic's own Alignment Science lead publicly stated his personal estimate that AI kills all humans is greater than 10% within the next decade — not a fringe view inside the lab, apparently.
The WeWorm exploit on WeChat calls succeeds even if the victim never answers — the phone doesn't need to be touched at all, and the call is silent if picked up.

OpenAI's Navier-Stokes team admitted they were 'inspired to pursue the problem after hearing a rumor' about two other researchers already working on it — one of whom was subsequently allegedly pressured off the paper for being Anthropic-affiliated.

Google's AlphaGenome Atlas processed 9 billion base-pair substitutions to annotate the functional consequence of every possible single-nucleotide change in the human genome — which is less than 3% protein-coding.

The NSA, CISA, and FBI allege Chinese AI firms ran coordinated prompt swarms of millions of queries against US frontier models — using bulk fake accounts — to distill frontier capabilities at a fraction of the training cost.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A film that operates as a meditation on memory, image-making, and how cultures encode time — Marker's essay-film form is the closest cinema gets to the kind of deep-structure thinking you live in, and the Japan/Guinea/Iceland triptych makes visible the invisible systems by which humans construct meaning from place. The 'zone' sequences, built from early video synthesis, still feel like someone describing the internet from 1983.

art_picks.title: Hiroshi Sugimoto — Theaters series
art_picks.creator: Hiroshi Sugimoto
art_picks.why: Each image is a single exposure for the entire runtime of a film — the screen burns to pure white, the architecture sits in perfect chiaroscuro, time becomes visible as accumulation. The conceptual apparatus is so clean it almost disappears; what's left is something that feels both like a system and like grief.

art_picks.title: Plat du Jour
art_picks.creator: Matmos
art_picks.why: An entire album of electronic music made exclusively from the sounds of food and agricultural processing — a ruthlessly formal conceptual constraint that somehow produces genuinely weird beauty. Matmos at their best are systems artists who happen to release records; this one is about industrial food supply and ends up sounding like a field recording from a dream.

events.name: Camille Henrot: Dogs
events.venue: Doris C. Freedman Plaza, Central Park (60th St. entrance)
events.why: Henrot's bronze dog sculptures aren't about dogs — they're about etiquette, control, and how societal rules shape imagination; each figure has its own idiosyncratic materiality and personality, a public installation that reads as both warm and structurally pointed about domestication.

events.name: Aziz Hazara: Coming Home
events.why: Hazara gathered literal tonnes of military consumer detritus abandoned at Bagram Airfield after the US withdrawal — kneepads, electronics, kitchenware — and is physically returning it to the US; the show is about supply chains, empire, and the everyday materiality of a twenty-year war, told entirely through objects.

events.name: Music for Action: Young the Giant / St. Lucia — Free Climate Week Concert
events.why: Free, open-air, first-come-first-served — a low-friction Tuesday night in the park with a band that actually delivers live; the climate-week framing is earnest but the music is the point.

events.name: Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony — Opening
events.why: The largest survey of Jafa's career — two floors of the newly expanded OMA building — featuring his full visual archive practice, where cinema, social media, news, and music are collaged into what he calls 'affective proximities' that expose how race is constructed and circulated through contemporary image culture.

events.name: The Armory Show 2026
events.why: The 2026 edition's Platform and Focus sections center artists from the Caribbean diaspora — less the blue-chip main floor, more the Presents section featuring galleries under 12 years old showing solo/dual presentations, which is where the actual live scouting happens.
